title: Bayes' Theorem with Several Causes
short: P(Aⱼ ∣ B) = P(B ∣ Aⱼ) P(Aⱼ) / Σ P(B ∣ Aᵢ) P(Aᵢ), and each new piece of evidence updates the answer again.
trouble: Students use P(B ∣ A) as if it were P(A ∣ B), or forget to divide by P(B).

blocks.html: In Bayes' rule you reversed a conditional probability with a tree. With several possible causes the idea is the same: the law of total probability supplies the denominator, and each cause gets its share. Bayes' theorem is how evidence updates a belief.

For a partition $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ and evidence $B$ with $P(B) > 0$: $$\role[posterior]{posterior}{P(A_j \mid B)} = \frac{\role[likelihood]{likelihood}{P(B \mid A_j)}\role[prior]{prior}{P(A_j)}}{\role[total probability of B]{evidence}{\sum_i P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)}}.$$ The posterior is proportional to prior × likelihood, rescaled so the posteriors add to 1.

By definition, $P(A_j \mid B) = \frac{P(A_j \cap B)}{P(B)}$. The numerator is $P(B \mid A_j)P(A_j)$ (the multiplication rule) and the denominator is $\sum_i P(B \mid A_i)P(A_i)$ (total probability). In tree language: among all the paths that end in B, the posterior of cause $A_j$ is the share of probability flowing through $A_j$.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: Given that the part is defective, only the three defective paths remain. Machine C has the highest defect rate, so its share of them is largest.

blocks.title: Which machine?
blocks.q: Machines A, B, C make 50%, 30%, 20% of the parts with defect rates 1%, 2%, 4%. A random part is defective. Find the probability that each machine made it.
steps: They add to 1. C makes the fewest parts but is the most likely source of a defect.

blocks.title: Two positive tests
blocks.q: A condition affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 95% of people with it and for 5% without it. A person tests positive twice, and the two results are independent given their condition. Find the probability they have the condition.
steps: $\approx 0.785$. One positive is weak evidence for a rare condition; two independent positives are much stronger. (A negative second result would instead multiply by $0.05$ on the "condition" side and $0.95$ on the other, pushing the probability back down.)

blocks.html: The same update in odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Here the prior odds are $\frac{1}{99}$, and each positive multiplies them by $\frac{0.95}{0.05} = 19$: after two positives the odds are $\frac{361}{99}$, a probability of $\frac{361}{460}$.

Reading the test's accuracy as the answer: $P(+ \mid \text{condition}) = 0.95$ is not $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$, which is only $0.161$ after one test. The other common slip is forgetting to divide by $P(B)$, so the "posteriors" do not add to 1. Check: list every cause and make sure your posteriors add to 1.
